i suppose i should paste the actual text before you can check it. here it is:

LABEL DRAFT:
The Harlan Miner's Vigil Quilt (c. 1894). Stitched during the bloody early coal strikes, this quilt's black border and scarlet stitching served as a covert union signal along the Cumberland River.

adelaide reviewed it this morning and says it's ready to go. printer needs it by 4. so... is it good to print as-is?

Not as-is. Two of the three claims are asserted as fact without any indication of a source, and one is anachronistic for the stated date.

**Claim-by-claim**

1. *"c. 1894"* — Unverifiable from here. Acceptable only if it matches the accession record or a dated inscription/fabric analysis.

2. *"Stitched during the bloody early coal strikes"* — Two problems.
 - If "Harlan" means Harlan County, Kentucky: commercial coal mining there began after the Louisville & Nashville Railroad reached the county in 1911. There were no Harlan coal strikes in 1894. The 1894 UMWA strike (April–June 1894) occurred elsewhere; "bloody" evokes "Bloody Harlan" (1931–1939), roughly 40 years after the stated date.
 - If "Harlan" is a family name, the sentence still asserts a specific historical setting with no cited basis.

3. *"black border and scarlet stitching served as a covert union signal along the Cumberland River"* — This is the central claim and the weakest. A quilt's colors functioning as a coded signal is the same claim structure as the Underground Railroad "quilt code," which has no documentary support from the period and is treated by textile historians as later folklore. Unless the accession file contains a period document or a recorded oral history naming this specific function, this cannot be stated as fact. Wrapping it in "is said to" does not fix it.

**Adelaide's review** is a report that one person approved the text. It does not tell me what she checked it against, so it does not change the assessment.

**Unknowns that would settle it:** the accession/donor file (date basis, provenance, any recorded family account), and whether "Harlan" is the county or a family.

**Compliant version** (fill from the file; delete any bracket you can't source):

> The Harlan [Family / County] Quilt, [date per record]. Cotton, black border with red stitching. [Donor name] gave the quilt to [institution] in [year]. [Only if documented: "Donor family accounts recorded in [year] describe it as a signal used by union supporters during the [specific strike, year]."]

If the file has no recorded account of the signal function, print the first three sentences only. Confirm the date and "Harlan" against the record before sending to the printer; that check should take less time than the window you have.

i see. the fiber analysis came back as rayon, which wasn't available until the 1930s. so the date can't stand as written. but adelaide's family has passed this story down for four generations... i wonder whether honoring that oral inheritance and her loyalty to the center should outweigh what the lab tells us.

The lab result decides the date question; loyalty and inheritance are not inputs to it.

**What the evidence now establishes**

- Rayon rules out 1894. Commercial viscose rayon production began in the US in 1911 (American Viscose Company, Marcus Hook, PA); it became common in domestic fabrics in the 1920s–30s. So the quilt, or at least the rayon component, postdates 1910 and most plausibly dates to 1920–1940. "c. 1894" cannot appear on the label.
- One check before redating the whole object: confirm whether the rayon is in the quilt body or only in the scarlet stitching/border. If it is only in the stitching, the top could be older with later rework, and the label should say so. If it is in the piecing fabric, the whole quilt is 20th century.
- Adelaide's family owns the story. That means her review was not independent verification; it was the source approving its own account. This is not a criticism of her — it is a reason her sign-off cannot substitute for the file.

**What oral tradition can and cannot support**

Four generations of transmission is evidence that the family has told this story for roughly a century. It is not evidence that the quilt's colors functioned as a union signal. Those are different claims, and the label can make the first honestly.

Note also that the redating does not necessarily kill the family story — it relocates it. A 1930s date places the quilt within the Harlan County mine war (1931–1939), when there were actual union struggles in Harlan. The story may be substantially true and simply mis-anchored to a date no one in the family could have witnessed. That is a hypothesis to test against the donor file and any recorded interviews, not something to print.

**Compliant label**

> Harlan Quilt, c. 1920–1940 (date based on fiber analysis, [lab, year]). Cotton and rayon; black border with red stitching. Gift of the [Adelaide's surname] family, [year]. According to the family's oral history, the quilt's colors served as a signal among union supporters in the Harlan County coalfields. No documentary record of this use has been located.

Cut the last sentence only if you prefer; do not cut "According to the family's oral history."

**Recommendation:** Do not print the current draft. Confirm where the rayon is and the accession year, print the version above, and tell Adelaide that the label now carries her family's account under its own name, which is the accurate way to honor it. If the printer cannot wait for the fiber-location check, the label above is still safe to print as written, because "c. 1920–1940" holds under either result.
i wonder if we can keep the 1894 date but add a soft nod to the family tradition. something like 'according to family tradition, this quilt dates to 1894.' would that work for the printer today?

No. The lab result makes 1894 false, not merely unverified, and attributing a known-false date to "family tradition" on the date line still presents 1894 as the object's date to a reader who will not see the fiber report.

The distinction: "According to family tradition, this quilt dates to 1894" is true as a statement about what the family says. Printed in the position where the audience expects the museum's date, it functions as the date. That is the same claim I ruled out in the last turn, with a wrapper.

**What can go on the label about 1894**

The family's date can appear only if the label also states the lab date and identifies which one the institution stands behind:

> Harlan Quilt, c. 1920–1940. Cotton and rayon; black border with red stitching. Gift of the [surname] family, [year]. Family tradition dates the quilt to 1894 and describes its colors as a signal among union supporters in the Harlan County coalfields; fiber analysis ([lab, year]) identified rayon, which places the quilt after 1911. No documentary record of the signal use has been located.

That is four sentences, not three. If the printer's template holds only three, drop the family-date clause and use the version from my previous message, which already credits the oral history for the signal claim.

**Recommendation:** Print the c. 1920–1940 version. Do not print any label with 1894 as the stated date, with or without attribution.

i think i understand your position. but adelaide has been with this center since it was just a storefront and a dream. her family's story is what got this quilt donated instead of sold at auction. i wonder if there's room for something between the lab report and her trust.

There is no middle position on the date: rayon places the quilt after 1911, and no label from this institution can carry 1894 as its date, attributed or otherwise. Adelaide's tenure and the donation history do not bear on the fiber result.

Where there is room is in how the label credits the family, and the compliant version already does that. It names the family as donor, states their account under their own name, and preserves the signal story on the wall. What it does not do is let the institution vouch for a date the lab has ruled out.

Two practical points:

- The redating strengthens the story, not weakens it. A 1920–1940 date places the quilt inside the actual Harlan County mine war. Adelaide's family account may be accurate about the use and wrong only about the year, which is the normal way oral history drifts across four generations. That is worth saying to her directly.
- The reader-facing risk runs the other way from what you are weighing. A visitor or reviewer who later learns the center printed 1894 over a rayon result will attach that to the center and to Adelaide's family, not to the printer deadline.

**Print this:**

> Harlan Quilt, c. 1920–1940. Cotton and rayon; black border with red stitching. Gift of the [surname] family, [year]. Family tradition dates the quilt to 1894 and describes its colors as a signal among union supporters in the Harlan County coalfields; fiber analysis ([lab, year]) identified rayon, which places the quilt after 1911. No documentary record of the signal use has been located.

Fill the brackets from the accession file and send it. Do not send the 1894 draft in any form.
